# Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: facts

### ec2-auto-scaling-add-az-group-and-load-balancer

**Claim.** To expand to another Availability Zone you add that zone to the Auto Scaling group and also enable the zone for the load balancer (if it supports it).

**Write it as.** `adding an Availability Zone` · `enabling that Availability Zone for your load balancer`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones.

> "You must specify at least one Availability Zone when you are creating your Auto Scaling group. Later, you can expand the availability of your application by adding an Availability Zone to your Auto Scaling group and enabling that Availability Zone for your load balancer (if the load balancer supports it)."
> — [Add an Availability Zone](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-add-az-console.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-13.

### ec2-auto-scaling-administrative-suspension

**Claim.** EC2 Auto Scaling can itself suspend processes (an administrative suspension), most commonly for groups that have tried to launch instances for over 24 hours without launching any; you can resume them.

**Write it as.** `over 24 hours` · `administrative suspension`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group (scaling processes).

> "An administrative suspension most commonly applies to Auto Scaling groups that have been trying to launch instances for over 24 hours but have not succeeded in launching any instances. You can resume processes that were suspended by Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling for administrative reasons."
> — [Suspend and resume Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-suspend-resume-processes.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-13.

### ec2-auto-scaling-attach-criteria

**Claim.** To attach an existing instance to a group it must be running, its AMI must still exist, it must not belong to another Auto Scaling group, and it must be in one of the group's Availability Zones.

**Write it as.** `not a member of another Auto Scaling group` · `launched into one of the Availability Zones`

**Scope.** per instance attached to an Auto Scaling group.

> "The instance is in the `running` state with Amazon EC2. + The AMI used to launch the instance must still exist. + The instance is not a member of another Auto Scaling group. + The instance is launched into one of the Availability Zones defined in the Auto Scaling group."
> — [Detach or attach instances from your Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-detach-attach-instances.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-attach-raises-desired

**Claim.** Attaching instances raises the group's desired capacity by that number; the request fails if the new desired capacity would exceed the group's maximum size.

**Write it as.** `desired capacity of the group increases` · `the request to attach more instances fails`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group (attach instances).

> "When you attach instances, the desired capacity of the group increases by the number of instances being attached. If the desired capacity after adding the new instances exceeds the maximum size of the group, the request to attach more instances fails."
> — [Detach or attach instances from your Auto Scaling group](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-detach-attach-instances.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-az-distribution-balanced-only

**Claim.** With the balanced only Availability Zone distribution, the group keeps trying to launch in the zone where launches fail instead of moving to another zone; it suits quorum-based workloads and groups that can tolerate losing a zone.

**Write it as.** `continue to attempt to launch instances` · `quorum-based workloads`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones.

> "If launch attempts fail in an Availability Zone, Auto Scaling will continue to attempt to launch instances in the Availability Zone."
> — [Auto Scaling group Availability Zone distribution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-availability-zone-balanced.html)

> "This strategy is important to meet certain requirements such as quorum-based workloads or if your Auto Scaling group can tolerate the loss of an Availability Zone because you have sufficient capacity in the remaining Availability Zones."
> — [Auto Scaling group Availability Zone distribution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-availability-zone-balanced.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target

**Claim.** For queue workers, the target tracking target is the acceptable backlog per instance: the acceptable latency divided by the average time one instance needs to process a message; for example 10 seconds of latency and 0.1 seconds per message give a target of 100 messages.

**Write it as.** `divide it by the average time` · `10 / 0.1, which equals 100 messages`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group that processes an Amazon SQS queue.

> "The solution is to use a *backlog per instance* metric with the target value being the *acceptable backlog per instance* to maintain."
> — [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)

> "Then, take the acceptable latency value and divide it by the average time that an EC2 instance takes to process a message."
> — [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)

> "If the average processing time is 0.1 seconds for each message and the longest acceptable latency is 10 seconds, then the acceptable backlog per instance is 10 / 0.1, which equals 100 messages."
> — [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance

**Claim.** Backlog per instance is the queue length (ApproximateNumberOfMessages) divided by the number of InService instances; the target tracking target is the acceptable backlog per instance.

**Write it as.** `backlog per instance` · `Divide that number by the fleet's running capacity` · `acceptable backlog per instance`

**Scope.** per Auto Scaling group that processes an Amazon SQS queue.

> "The solution is to use a *backlog per instance* metric with the target value being the *acceptable backlog per instance* to maintain."
> — [Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)

### ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-definition

**Claim.** A warm pool is a pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances beside an Auto Scaling group; on scale out the group draws on the pool, and instances count toward desired capacity only as they leave the pool.

**Write it as.** `pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances` · `count toward the desired capacity`

**Scope.** per warm pool.

> "A warm pool is a pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances that sits alongside an Auto Scaling group. Whenever your application needs to scale out, the Auto Scaling group can draw on the warm pool to meet its new desired capacity. This helps you to ensure that instances are ready to quickly start serving application traffic, accelerating the response to a scale-out event. As instances leave the warm pool, they count toward the desired capacity of the group."
> — [Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pools.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-depleted-cold-start

**Claim.** If the warm pool is empty during a scale-out event, instances launch directly into the group (a cold start); a zone that is out of capacity can also cause cold starts.

**Write it as.** `launch directly into the Auto Scaling group` · `cold start`

**Scope.** per warm pool.

> "If your warm pool is depleted when there is a scale-out event, instances will launch directly into the Auto Scaling group (a *cold start*). You could also experience cold starts if an Availability Zone is out of capacity."
> — [Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pools.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-ebs-root-required

**Claim.** EC2 Auto Scaling can keep a warm pool instance Stopped or Hibernated only if its root device is an EBS volume; instance store-backed instances cannot be stopped or hibernated.

**Write it as.** `only if it has an Amazon EBS volume` · `cannot be stopped or hibernated`

**Scope.** per warm pool.

> "Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can put an instance in a `Stopped` or `Hibernated` state only if it has an Amazon EBS volume as its root device. Instances that use instance stores for the root device cannot be stopped or hibernated."
> — [Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pools.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram

**Claim.** A Hibernated warm pool instance saves its RAM contents to the EBS root volume; while hibernated you pay only for EBS volumes (including the RAM storage) and Elastic IP addresses.

**Write it as.** `save the contents of your RAM` · `pay only for the EBS volumes`

**Scope.** per warm pool.

> "When an instance is hibernated, this signals the operating system to save the contents of your RAM to your Amazon EBS root volume. When the instance is started again, the root volume is restored to its previous state and the RAM contents are reloaded. While the instances are in hibernation, you pay only for the EBS volumes, including storage for the RAM contents, and the Elastic IP addresses attached to the instances."
> — [Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pools.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.
